extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners in software-related arts (including AI/ML) — Technology Centers 2100, 2600, 3600
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for patent examiners on analyzing claim subject matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 101, with emphasis on software and AI/ML claims and application of the USPTO MPEP flowchart (Step 2A Prong One/Two and related considerations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI)
rubrics_metrics.description: The broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim must be established prior to examining a claim for eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should determine BRI before performing eligibility analysis (see MPEP 2106, subsection II). BRI is the baseline for applying the flowchart in MPEP 2106, subsection III.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow MPEP 2106 flowchart for eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether a claim satisfies subject matter eligibility criteria by following the flowchart provided in MPEP 2106, subsection III.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the official flowchart (updated in the AI-SME Update to reference Alice/Mayo Steps 1 and 2 and include a dotted line around Step 2A). Consult MPEP 2103–2106.07 for detailed guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong One — does the claim recite a judicial exception?
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether a claim recites a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO distills relevant case law into three enumerated groupings of abstract ideas: mathematical concepts, certain methods of organizing human activity, and mental processes (see MPEP 2106.04(a)). If the claim sets forth or describes such an exception, further analysis is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental process grouping — definition and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A mental process (thinking) that 'can be performed in the human mind, or by a human using a pen and paper,' is treated as an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine a claim recites a mental process when it contains limitations that can practically be performed in the human mind (e.g., observations, evaluations, judgments, opinions). Do NOT expand this grouping to encompass limitations that cannot practically be performed in the human mind; limitations that encompass AI in a way the human mind cannot practically perform do not fall in this grouping. See AI-SME Update and MPEP examples showing hardware-based limitations that are not mental processes (e.g., uniquely encoded RFID transponder data structures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish 'recites' vs 'involves' a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that 'recite' an exception (set forth or describe it) require further eligibility analysis; claims that merely 'involve' an exception (are based on it) may be eligible and not require further analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult MPEP 2106.04, subsection II(A)(1) for the recite vs involve distinction and Ex Parte Linden for PTAB considerations. Use concrete claim language analysis to decide whether the exception is recited (described) or merely involved (based on).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete examples to identify recitation (e.g., Example 39 vs 47)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply example-based reasoning: a limitation like 'training the neural network' may merely involve an abstract idea, whereas naming specific mathematical algorithms (e.g., backpropagation, gradient descent) can recite a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare USPTO examples: Example 39 (Method for Training a Neural Network for Facial Detection) — limitation 'training the neural network in a first stage using the first training set' does not recite an exception; Example 47 (Anomaly Detection) — limitation specifying backpropagation and gradient descent recites a mathematical abstract idea. Use examples to guide whether claim language describes mathematical relationships/calculations explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong Two — does the claim integrate the exception into a practical application?
rubrics_metrics.description: After a claim is found to recite a judicial exception, evaluate whether the claim as a whole integrates the recited exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the considerations in MPEP 2106.04(d) to evaluate whether additional elements integrate the exception into a practical application. Many considerations overlap and multiple may apply. Not all considerations will be relevant to every element or claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze the claim as a whole and consider interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating integration into a practical application, consider all claim limitations and how they interact and impact each other — do not evaluate additional limitations in a vacuum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The way additional elements use or interact with the exception can integrate the exception into a practical application. Consider combined effect of limitations rather than isolating them. See MPEP 2106.04(d), subsection III.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements consideration — improvement to computer or technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims can be eligible if they reflect an improvement to the functioning of a computer or to another technology or technical field, integrating the judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the claim covers a particular solution to a problem or a particular way to achieve an outcome rather than merely claiming the idea of a solution. Consult the specification to determine whether the disclosed invention improves technology; the specification need not explicitly state the improvement but must describe the invention such that the improvement would be apparent to a person of ordinary skill. The claim itself does not have to explicitly recite the improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Apply it' consideration — more than mere instructions to implement
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether additional elements amount to more than a recitation of the words 'apply it' (or equivalent) — mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer are not sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not oversimplify claim limitations when applying the 'apply it' consideration. This consideration often overlaps with the improvements consideration. Assess whether the claim provides meaningful limiting detail beyond a generic instruction to use a computer to perform the judicial exception. See MPEP 2106.05(f) and warning not to expand 'apply it' too broadly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity vs generality when assessing 'apply it' and improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the particularity or generality of how the judicial exception is applied: does the claim recite only the idea/outcome, or a particular solution/way to achieve it?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating additional elements, consider: (1) whether the claim recites only the idea of a solution or provides details of how the solution is accomplished; (2) whether the claim invokes computers/machinery merely as a tool or purports to improve computer capabilities or existing technology; (3) the particularity or generality of the application. Claims that improve computer capabilities or technology support finding the exception is integrated into a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid oversimplification of claim limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners must be careful not to oversimplify the claims by looking at them generally and failing to account for the specific requirements of the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider all claim limitations (see MPEP 2106.05(a) and MPEP 2143.03). Overbroad simplification can lead to incorrect 'apply it' conclusions; analyze specific requirements and how they limit the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other judicial considerations at Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B
rubrics_metrics.description: There are additional judicial considerations (beyond improvements and 'apply it') that may be relevant at Step 2A Prong Two or at Step 2B (inventive concept).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP 2106.04(d)(2) and 2106.05(b)-(e), (g)-(h) for lists of other judicial considerations to evaluate whether additional elements integrate an exception into a practical application or amount to an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for making a subject matter eligibility (SME) rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Only make a SME rejection when it is more likely than not (>50%) that the claim is ineligible under 35 U.S.C. 101; unpatentability must be established by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If it's a 'close call' as to eligibility, do not make a rejection unless the examiner finds it more likely than not the claim is ineligible. This standard applies across statutory bases per MPEP 706(I). Do not reject merely because of uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact prosecution and complete examination of other grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Regardless of whether an SME rejection is made in a first Office action, a complete examination should be made for every claim under other patentability requirements (35 U.S.C. 102, 103, 112).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the first Office action, state all non‑cumulative reasons and bases for rejecting claims. Do not omit examination of other statutory bases just because of an eligibility question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use USPTO training materials and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should consult the MPEP, the AI-SME Update, and the July 2024 Subject Matter Eligibility Examples (and earlier examples) for further explanation and illustrative analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training modules (introductory and advanced) and example sets are available on the 35 U.S.C. 101 intranet webpage and USPTO SME internet webpage. Use these resources to apply the guidance and see concrete example analyses (e.g., Examples 37–42, Example 47).
